p: Steuart's Confederate brigade makes repeated assaults up the steep hill. 1st Maryland Confederate and 3rd NC suffer heavy casualties. The parallel fight between Union and Confederate Maryland regiments is ongoing here.

Colgrove's controversial charge. Mudge's 2nd Massachusetts and 27th Indiana ordered to charge across an open meadow toward Confederate positions. Mudge's last words: 'It is murder but it is the order.' Mudge killed leading the charge.
Both sides fight a grinding attritional battle on Culp's Hill. Johnson's Confederates make twelve distinct assaults. XII Corps holds the upper works throughout. Confederate ammunition running low.
XII Corps counterattacks aggressively. Candy's, Kane's, and Greene's brigades advance to recapture lower works. Johnson's division slowly pushed back. Steuart's brigade suffering severely.

p.short: Site chronology, Day 3 (Culp's Hill lower works)

p: Johnson's Confederate assault on Culp's Hill exhausted. Confederate ammunition nearly expended. Johnson signals Ewell that he cannot continue. Ewell orders Johnson to hold what he has.

Pickett's fresh division moves up behind Seminary Ridge in preparation for the afternoon assault. The three Virginia brigades (Garnett, Kemper, Armistead) form in the woods, invisible to Union observers.

Pettigrew's division (Heth's old command) and Trimble's two brigades (Lane and Scales/Lowrance) positioned on Seminary Ridge left of Pickett. The assault force numbers approximately 12,500 men across a mile front.
Final Culp's Hill fighting. XII Corps retakes most of the contested works. Johnson's remaining Confederates hold a small section of the lower works but are effectively contained.

Culp's Hill fighting finally ends at approximately 11:00am. Johnson's division retires. Twelve Confederate assaults repulsed. Union line on Culp's Hill completely restored. Total Culp's Hill casualties: approximately 3,500 across both days.
The seven-hour Culp's Hill fight was the longest sustained infantry battle of Gettysburg but is overshadowed by Pickett's Charge in popular memory.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (chronology commentary)

p: Alexander positions the Confederate artillery along Seminary Ridge for the cannonade. 170 Confederate guns arranged in a two-mile arc from the Peach Orchard north to the Hagerstown Road. Alexander writes two famous messages to Pickett.

THE CANNONADE BEGINS. At approximately 1:00pm, two Confederate signal guns fire in sequence. 170 Confederate guns open fire simultaneously — the largest artillery bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere to that date. The sound is heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away.
Alexander later wrote that the cannonade was the most magnificent spectacle he ever witnessed. The Union artillery chief Hunt deliberately slowed Union counter-fire to conserve ammunition.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (chronology commentary)

p: Hunt deliberately silences Union artillery to conserve ammunition for the infantry assault. Hancock overrules Hunt and orders the guns to keep firing for morale. The disagreement between Hunt and Hancock shapes the eventual repulse.
Hunt's decision to conserve ammunition was tactically correct. Hancock's decision to keep firing boosted infantry morale but depleted artillery reserves.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (chronology commentary)

p: Confederate artillery fire overshooting Cemetery Ridge — most shells landing behind the Union line near Taneytown Road. Union artillery casualties lighter than expected. Meade's headquarters nearly hit.

p.short: Site chronology, Day 3 (Cemetery Ridge / Taneytown Road)
